hypothesis.title: Measure whether any score_runnable multiplier can outvote the random priority draw
hypothesis.description: Take the mechanism already in tree -- quick_fire_multiplier on a Recover whose node is crashed -- and sweep it over decades (1, 3, 10, 100, 1000) on scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json, recording per-value the fraction of selections in which the reweighted branch actually changed which runnable was picked versus the unweighted ordering. This needs a selection-order comparison counter in scheduler.rs (compute the argmax with and without the multiplier, count disagreements) plus util_stats counters multiplier_authority.{decisions, flipped}; it needs no new policy and no new config key beyond reusing the existing multiplier. Report the flip rate as a function of multiplier magnitude.
hypothesis.rationale: score_runnable is 0.25*novelty + 0.75*priority with priority a random draw fixed at runnable creation. Two hypotheses have now died on this surface (timer-vs-delivery-coverage-axis, starvation-gated-timer-admission) and in neither case do we know whether the intervention reached the decision. If a 100x multiplier flips selection in only a percent or two of decisions, structural reweighting of score_runnable is a dead axis and all future timer/crash/delivery-admission work must intervene at enqueue or admission time rather than at scoring -- which redirects the whole scheduler category rather than retiring one more knob. If flip rates are high, then the two nulls were real nulls and the axis stays open.
hypothesis.generalityArgument: The question is about the arithmetic of the scheduler's own selection rule, not about any protocol. It asks whether a term of a given magnitude can dominate a uniform random term of weight 0.75 -- an answer that holds for VR, for any other spec, and for any mechanism that would reweight the same sum.
